'''''Melaleuca styphelioides''''', known as the '''prickly-leaved paperbark''' or '''prickly paperbark''', is a plant native to eastern [[Australia]]. It is a tree with spongy bark, prickly leaves and spikes of creamy-white flowers.

==Description==
It is a small to medium-sized tree up to {{convert|20|m|ft|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} high with a dense, rounded canopy and drooping branchlets.<ref name=NSW/><ref name=Cronin/> The spongy bark is white or light brown and peels off in large strips.<ref name=Cronin>{{cite book|author=Cronin, Leonard| title=A Concise Australian Flora |publisher=Reed Books|location= | year=1989| isbn=0730102920}}</ref> The leaves are [[Sessility (botany)|sessile]], {{convert|7-15|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|2.5-6|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} wide.<ref name=NSW>{{cite web |url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Melaleuca~styphelioides |title=''Melaleuca styphelioides'' |accessdate=2009-11-03 |author= |work=PlantNET - New South Wales Flora Online |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens & Domain Trust, Sydney Australia |archive-date=2008-08-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080817184903/http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Melaleuca~styphelioides |url-status=live }}</ref>  They are slightly twisted, have sharply-pointed tips, are arranged alternately on the branchlets and have between 15 and 30 veins.<ref name=Cronin/><ref name=Brophy>{{cite book|last1=Brophy|first1=Joseph J.|last2=Craven|first2=Lyndley A.|last3=Doran|first3=John C.|title=Melaleucas : their botany, essential oils and uses|date=2013|publisher=Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research|location=Canberra|isbn=9781922137517|pages =345–346}}</ref>

Flowers appear in summer in cream or white cylindrical "bottlebrush" spikes which are {{convert|2 to 5|cm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|1 to 2|cm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} in diameter. Often new growth appears at the end of the spikes.<ref name=Cronin/> Following flowering, grey-brown, woody [[Capsule (botany)|capsules]] appear in clusters along the branchlets. These are ovoid, stalkless and {{convert|3 to 4|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} in diameter<ref name=Cronin/>[[File:Melaleuca styphelioides habit.jpg|thumb|225px|Habit near [[Newcastle, New South Wales|Newcastle]]]]

==Taxonomy==
The species was first formally described in 1797 by botanist [[James Edward Smith (botanist)|James Edward Smith]] in ''[[Transactions of the Linnean Society of London]]'' from plant material collected by [[David Burton (botanist)|David Burton]] near [[Port Jackson]].<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Melaleuca styphelioides''|url=  https://biodiversity.org.au/boa/instance/apni/544413|publisher=APNI|accessdate=23 July 2015}}</ref> The [[Botanical name|specific epithet]] (''styphelioides'') refers to the  similarity of the leaves of this species with those of a plant in the genus ''[[Styphelia]]'' in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Ericaceae]].<ref name="Brophy" />

==Distribution and habitat==
The species occurs along stream banks or other moist situations, mostly in coastal areas from [[Nowra]] in [[New South Wales]] and northwards in to [[Queensland]].<ref name=NSW/>

==Use in horticulture==
This melaleuca thrives in a variety of situations ranging from swampy to hot and dry, and due to its deep-rooting characteristics lawn can be grown under its canopy.<ref name=Lord>{{cite book|author=Lord, E|author2=J.H.Willis| title=Shrubs and trees for Australian gardens| publisher=Lothian|location= Australia | year=1982 | isbn=0850910277}}</ref> It is used as a street tree in [[Sydney]], with good examples in [[Campsie, New South Wales|Campsie]], an inner southwestern suburb, and also along numerous streets in various suburbs of Greater [[Melbourne]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Frank |first1=Stephen |last2=Waters |first2=Glen |last3=Beer |first3=Russell |last4=May |first4=Peter |year=2006 |title=An Analysis of the Street Tree Population of Greater Melbourne at the Beginning of the 21st Century |journal=Arboriculture & Urban Forestry |volume=32 |issue=4 |pages=155–163 |publisher=International Society of Arboriculture |doi=10.48044/jauf.2006.021 |s2cid=55146575 |url=http://treelogic.com.au/facts/wp-content/uploads/2009/09/S.Frank.pdf |accessdate=4 October 2013}}</ref>
